newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai budget cuts seen ushering economic stability.
newsitem.headline: Thai budget cuts seen ushering economic stability.

text.p: The Thai government's decision on Tuesday to make sweeping spending cuts for fiscal 1996/97 ending in September will bring much-needed economic stability but curb growth, analysts said.

The cuts totalling 99 billion baht ($3.8 billion) will push 1997 gross domestic product growth below the revised 6.8 percent projected by the Bank of Thailand (BOT) governor Rerngchai Marakanond from 7.1 percent anticipated earlier, they said.

But despite the expected slowdown, analysts told Reuters the cuts would bring much-needed stability by reducing Thailand's wide current account deficit which could subsequently relieve pressure on the current tight monetary policy.
Thai rates are being held at high levels by the BOT to curb speculation in the weak baht which was recently hit by a surging dollar, central bank officials said.

"In principle, we agree with the tightening of fiscal policy as it is the most effective measure to improve the country's sizeable external imbalance," said Arporn Chewakrenkai of Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
"But the cuts accounted for approximately two percent of the GDP, therefore the impact on the economic growth could be higher than that projected by the central bank," she said.
She forecast that the latest cuts would slow economic growth by 0.4-0.8 percent but narrow the current account deficit by 1.0-1.5 percent to 6.5-7.0 percent of GDP.
Rerngchai had said the cuts could narrow the 1997 current account deficit to 7.4 percent of GDP from an earlier projection of 7.9 percent.
Of the total cut, 59 billion will be from the annual budget to help counter shortfalls in revenue which is expected to slide to 925 billion baht from 984 billion projected earlier.
In addition, the government will also slash state enterprises investment by 40 billion baht.
Prime Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh had said earlier pledged that the cut would be imposed on low-return projects which would not negatively affect economic growth.
Paul Alapat of Lehman Brothers saw the BOT's new forecast on GDP growth as being too optimistic but said the spending cuts were a move in the right direction.

Alapat pointed out that this particular cut was unlikely to have substantial impact on the economic growth as the cuts were believed to be in low-return sectors such as spending in defence and transport.
But he expressed doubt that the government would meet the revenue target, and may be forced to cut spending once again and consequently slow down the economy.
Lehman Brothers forecast that 1997 GDP growth will be at 6.0 percent and the current account deficit at 6.9 percent of GDP.
"This is a very positive move. But again we have to see how it is going to be implemented and how well it is put into action," he said.
